summary: Describes how a DNS resolver can run a copy of the root zone on a loopback address to get faster answers and to keep requests from being observed. It explains how to set up and maintain such a copy safely. It was replaced by RFC 8806.

eli5.summary: Instead of phoning far away for a directory, you keep a copy at home. It was replaced by RFC 8806.

subtitle: How a resolver can keep its own copy of the DNS root zone on a loopback address, and why the RFC warns against doing it lightly.

tldr.problem: Some DNS resolvers have a slow path to the nearest root server, and some operators do not want third parties to see their root queries.
tldr.mechanism: Run an authoritative server holding a full copy of the root zone on a loopback address of the same host, keep it refreshed from the SOA timers, and point the resolver at it while still validating answers with DNSSEC.
tldr.outcome: It speeds up and hides mostly negative root lookups, but adds operational fragility. The RFC says this is not a best practice, and it has been obsoleted by RFC 8806.

sections.title: Why Keep the Root Zone Nearby
sections.content:
A recursive resolver must answer every query from its customers, even for names that do not exist. For each top-level domain (TLD) that is not in its cache, it has to ask a root server. Most queries that reach the root are for names that are not in the root zone, and negative answers are cached for a much shorter time. A slow path to the nearest root server therefore hurts the resolver's customers.

Those queries can also be watched by malicious third parties on the network between the resolver and the roots. The document proposes a copy of the root zone on a loopback address on the same host as the resolver, so answers come back quickly and the queries are not visible on the network.
sections.eli5: Asking a faraway helper the same question over and over is slow, and others might overhear you. Keeping a copy of the answers in your own room fixes both problems.

sections.title: Goals, Non-Goals and Warnings
sections.content:
The main goals are faster negative responses to junk queries from stub resolvers and keeping queries and responses off the network. Faster positive responses are explicitly a non-goal, because data for real TLDs is long-lived and usually already cached.

The server is allowed only on a loopback address, so it cannot give authoritative answers to any system other than the resolver itself.

The RFC states that this design is not considered a best practice. Many people regard it as excessively risky because it adds a new operational piece. If it breaks, users can get bad data or resolution can fail in hard-to-diagnose ways. Distributions of recursive DNS servers MUST NOT include configuration for it.
sections.eli5: This trick helps with silly or misspelled questions, not with common ones. It is also easy to get wrong, so the authors say not to switch it on without reading the warnings.

sections.title: What the System Must Have
sections.content:
To use the mechanism, the system MUST be able to validate a zone with DNSSEC, have an up-to-date copy of the DNS root key, be able to retrieve the entire root zone including all DNSSEC-related records, and be able to run an authoritative server on a loopback address (an address in 127/8 for IPv4, or ::1 in IPv6).

The data in the local root zone MUST be identical to the real root zone. Glue records are unsigned and could be changed, but that could cause problems, so they SHOULD NOT be changed.
sections.eli5: Your copy has to be an exact copy, and you must be able to check that it is genuine. Scribbling changes on it is a bad idea.

sections.title: Running and Refreshing the Local Root
sections.content:
Setup has two steps: retrieve a copy of the root zone, then start the authoritative server with that zone on an unused loopback address. For IPv4 this is typically 127.0.0.1, but any address in 127/8 will do. For IPv6 it is ::1. The resolver is then told to look at that address when it needs root information, and it validates every answer with DNSSEC as it would for a remote root server.

The zone MUST be refreshed using the timers in the root zone's SOA record. If it cannot be refreshed before the expire time, the server MUST return SERVFAIL for all queries until the zone is set up again. A failed refresh can be disastrous, for example if all the NS records for a TLD change within a short period such as 2 days.

Operators SHOULD have an automated check that the local zone is being refreshed, for example by checking that its SOA keeps changing. At the time of writing the root SOA was the date with a two-digit counter appended and changed every day; on January 2, 2015 it was 2015010201.

To test the setup, send the recursive server a query for the root SOA and check that the AA bit in the response header is 0.
sections.eli5: A stale copy is dangerous, like using an old phone book after everyone moved. So the copy must be re-checked on a schedule, and if it gets too old it must say 'I do not know' instead of guessing.

sections.title: Security and Operational Risk
sections.content:
A system that skips the DNSSEC requirements can be fooled into giving bad answers, just like any resolver that does not validate responses from a remote root server. Keeping the server on loopback limits the damage to other systems that might otherwise rely on an altered copy of the root.

The appendices show example configurations for BIND 9.9, Unbound 1.4 with NSD 4, and Microsoft Windows Server 2012. With BIND the two roles share fate, so if the root server dies, BIND is likely dead too. With Unbound and NSD they are separate, so the administrator should monitor NSD and restart it immediately. Appendix A lists places the root zone could be fetched by AXFR over TCP, and warns that none are guaranteed to stay available.
sections.eli5: The copy lives only inside your own computer, so it cannot mislead anyone else. If the helper program that holds it stops working, though, you need to notice quickly.
